segments.text: Please welcome Luca on stage who will talk about performance optimization on front end especially on mobile which is sometimes becoming tricky. Yeah. Yep. So uh thank you all for being here. So,
I'm Luca and quick context, uh, I'm a front end developer on the Adobe Fonts team and we bring over 35,000 fonts to all Adobe products. And one of those
products is Adobe Express. And if you haven't heard of it, uh, it's like a creative app for everyone. Like you can make social media posts, uh, flyers,
short videos, presentations. So, you know, it's designed to be easy even if you're not a designer. and it runs entirely on the web. Uh our
team built a font recommendations component inside express. On desktop, it appears the moment uh you select the text element on the left side of the
screen. On mobile, uh you select the text element, you tap on the fonts button, and the panel slides up. So, you know, the user has to actively open it
and that's going to be important later for a feature like this. Uh performance is everything. I mean if it takes too long to show those fonts uh you've
broken the creative flow. Uh the user you know had an idea, they tapped and now they are waiting. Uh so that's one of the worst things that you can do in a
creative tool. So you know we've been building this feature for about a year and we made the strategic decision to prioritize the user experience and ship
the feature first with a plan to address performance in a subsequent phase. or you know uh we decided to launch first and fix performance later and when the
data came back we saw just how big the task was. Uh but first quickly uh here's how we measure performance. So we use percentiles. Uh P50 is your median user
and P90 is the slowest 10%. We color code each against our targets. So green if you're hitting it, uh, red if you're way over.
Our P50 on Android was already three times over target. So it was red. And the P90, so your slowest users, maybe on an older phone or or, you know, a bad
connection, uh, it was nearly double its target. So it was just unusable. And that's the mountain that we had to climb. And the story of how we got to
the top uh is what I want to share today. And it really started from a place of not having any great ideas. So in fact
when the problem first came to me, my very first thought was like honestly how much can I even do here? Uh because I was pretty sure that the fix wasn't
going to come from me from the front end. Uh I had worked on this component for about a year so I knew it pretty
well. Under the hood, there are three steps. So, first we fetch the recommendation. Uh it's an API that takes like context from the document uh
and returns a list of fonts that would be a good fit. The fonts come back as technical names. So, the next step is to you know map
them to useful metadata like the display name, the style name if they are premium and so on. And third, we need to, you know, actually show those fonts. And on
mobile, that means downloading a small preview image for each one. So, you know, that was my mental model. It's like basically chaining a bunch of API
calls together. You know, step one, step two, step three, you know, all sequential, all dependent on the previous one. So, if it's slow, it has
to be the back end, right? Uh and that's and you know when I opened Chrome DevTools everything I saw just confirmed this idea like I saw these big
empty spaces uh where the main thread was you know just idle waiting for the API calls to finish. So my conclusion was simple the front end is fine so
that also meant that I was you know completely stuck like for a few days I didn't know how to move forward. I just kept looking at the code, you know,
hoping to see something new. And then the first clue came from a completely unexpected place. So I was taking an online course on web
development. It covered a lot of deep topics, but one lesson stuck with me. Uh it was about something called cross origin resource sharing or course. So
you know the instructor explained that uh when your JavaScript makes a request to a different domain uh that's a cross origin request the browser has a
decision to make. So if the request is what the spec calls a simple request uh so basically you know playing get with only standard headers the browser just
sends it like no questions asked. But the moment you do something that the browser considers non-standard like you know adding a custom header, it gets
cautious. So before sending your actual request, it first sends a tiny options request uh to the server like asking is this allowed and that's called the
pre-flight. Only after it gets the okay does the browser you know send your real request. So uh one logical request from your code become two uh network round trips.
And as the instructor was explaining all of this uh something started nagging at me like that word uh pre-flight I knew it like I had seen it in our network tab
so many times. Uh every single one of our API calls had this you know extra request sitting right above it. I just assumed it was you know normal some
technical thing that the browser had to do. I never once questioned it but now I was thinking like wait uh we are just fetching data. This should be the
simplest request possible. So why is the browser treating our request as non-standard? So I went back uh and I looked at our request headers
and there it was. Uh we were sending a client identifier via custom header. So it was something like uh x API key. It just told the server like which
application was calling. But the browser, you know, doesn't care what it's for. Custom header is a custom header. Uh and that single header, you
know, was enough to make every one of our get requests non simple. The browser had been, you know, dutifully adding a pre-flight to every single API call and
had been doing so for about a year. So I checked with the backend team and here's the funny part like the API already supported sending that key as a query
parameter like in the URL instead of a request header the whole time. You know the option was you know right there in the documentation. We just never used
it. So we moved the key to the URL and that's it. Like the browser saw like a plain get with no custom headers. uh it
classified it as a simple request and stopped you know sending those pre-flights. So just like that we saved 200 milliseconds with a 5minut fix.
It wasn't the biggest fix. Uh but for me it was you know super important. Uh it was like the first proof that my assumption was wrong. uh it showed that
there were things that I could fix and this was also my first big lesson like performance problems uh often live at the boundary between front end and
back end uh and you know this first small win also gave me some confidence but it also made me realize something like I'd been staring at those
pre-flights uh for a year and never questioned them so what else was I not seeing I started looking at a startup step in our code. So it was like a blocking call
that you know among other things it was checking if the user was premium or not. I was feeling pretty confident on this one. I thought I thought like this is
not a big deal on mobile. We have like a system that pre-initializes this check before the panel even opens. So you know by the time the component is actually
shown it should be instant. So, you know, I was so confident I just put the ticket back in the backlog and uh moved on.
But, you know, that lesson from the previous issue like just kept nagging at me like you know check the data. Uh so I did and I checked our analytics and the
results were shocking. So, uh for the median user, yeah, my intuition was spot on. Almost zero time spent on this startup step. But for our P90 users, it
was a completely different story. Like this instance step was taking almost a full second on Android. Like it was eating half of our performance budget.
So you know my gut feeling was wrong. Once again I spent a day you know trying to optimize that startup code but it was a
dead end. Uh the code was also too risky to change I thought. However, uh the next day I realized something. So instead of focusing on how
to fix the slow startup code, uh I started thinking about what it was actually doing. And the part that was taking the most time was, as I said,
checking if the user was paid. So I realized that the host app, so Adobe Express itself already has that information. like of course is it does
it's like the app the user is signed into. We are a separate library that's embedded inside it which is probably why that never occurred to us. So the fix
was really simple actually like just ask the host app for the paid state directly. It was like a tiny change on our side but it completely removed uh
you know that blocking network call and all the performance problems that came with it. This saved another 400 milliseconds uh making it our biggest fix uh yet and it
came uh you know just from looking at the problem from a different angle. That same shift in perspective uh is what led me straight to the next
discovery. But to understand this next part, you need to understand what happens when uh or before a network request is even sent. So when your browser, you know, needs to
talk to a domain, it can't just send a request. So first it it needs to find the the IP address. So that's the DNS
lookup. And if it's not cached, uh that alone can take, you know, 100 milliseconds or more on mobile, let's say. then uh you know it needs to
establish a secure connection uh the TCP TLS and check and that's maybe another 100 to 150 milliseconds on mobile and the key thing is that you pay this cost
per origin so if you need to talk to two different domains you do this whole dance twice and you know only then does your actual
request go through in our network waterfall. So I saw that we were making two API calls but they were going to two different domains. So
you know that meant two separate connections, two handshakes and when your total time budget is half a second thing possibly 150 millconds twice is
you know a lot. So my first instinct as a front- end engineer was to try and fix it on the client. Uh I just learned
about a feature that was called uh resource hints. Uh, and that's how you can tell the browser like, hey, I'm going to need this soon. Please start
the connection. Now, I spent the whole day trying to make it work, adding the hint text dynamically, like the moment our component is uh mounted, uh, it
appears on the screen. It felt clever, but uh, it didn't work reliably. The next day uh I realized that I was still thinking too small like still
trying to keep the problem in uh my world. It took me a while to get there, but eventually, you know, I went to the
back end team and asked a simple question like, could they move the second API so it's on the same CDN as the first one? You know, that would mean
one shared origin instead of two and you know they did. And this saved about 270 milliseconds. So, uh, at this point I was feeling pretty
good. You know, we were making real progress, but then I looked at the new performance data from the last fix and I saw something that made absolutely no
sense. Like the API that was moved was faster, yes, but the time spent client side had actually gone up by 250 milliseconds. Like it was completely
counterintuitive. So, you know, I looked into it and that API's job is to serve preview images for the fonts, but it also has a fallback
like if it fails, we download the font file instead. But, you know, how would that explain the client side time going up? It didn't make any sense. So, uh I dug
deeper into our analytics. This time running a group uh query group by country you know just to see if there are any patterns and the result was
shocking like in almost every every country users were getting image previews as expected but in one major region like 100% of our users were getting the fallback instead
like 100%. So, you know, that couldn't be a coincidence. It meant that for an entire region, our primary API was failing every single time, forcing every
single user into the slower backup path. Okay, but why did the client side time go up in my reports? Well, it's because our analytics code
was wrong. It turns out uh we were timing only the final successful download. like all the time spent waiting for the first attempt to fail
was invisible to us like so it got silently lumped into the client side slice so one of the numbers that I trusted the most in my own reports was you know
simply wrong so it's a good reminder when you see surprising data maybe also question your measurement so anyway you know once we understood what was
actually happening fixing it was easy like the CDN just needing needed a configuration changed for that region and between the consolidation and this fix uh we saved about 720 milliseconds
combined. Uh this investigation also taught me that with when you are focused on performance even a simple bug fix can have unintended consequences like uh at
one point I was looking through our mobile code and I noticed something that you know looked like an obvious oversight. So, we wanted to show 12 fonts in our
panel, but we were asking the API for just four up front, you know, the same number we used on desktop. Then making a second API call to get the other eight.
So, you know, I saw it and I thought, great, easy win. Wrote a fix to request all 12 at once and it got merged.
A few days later, I realized something. So, the API that returns the fonts sits behind the CDN. So this means that responses are cached and our desktop
component appears every time you select a text. So of course desktop has far more uh traffic than mobile by asking for just four fonts on mobile like the
same number as desktop. Our mobile users were accidentally writing this massive cache being built by all those desktop users. and my fix would have made the
mobile request unique and mobile would have stopped hitting that worm cache entirely. So, you know, performance would have gotten worse. So, uh I rushed
to re revert my own change, you know, just before it was released. But the lesson was humbling. You know, what looks like a bug might just be, you
know, an accidental performance feature. So, you have to be so so careful. And I made another mistake in the same spirit. So around the same time, we got
a product request which was basically show localized preview text for users in certain regions instead of the default the quick brown fox. This made total
sense like all I had to do was send the users local as a new parameter to that image preview API. You know, a small
change. I shipped it quickly. What I didn't realize was that I had just fragmented our CDN cache like 40 times over. So we now have one cache
preview per font per local. Since this parameter was sent on every single request, the entire existing cache became useless overnight. Now that's nothing permanent. You know, the cache
rebuilds over time. But adding a cache heavy feature right in the middle of a performance investigation maybe not my best timing you know so the
lesson from both like even a well-intentioned change can have side effects that you don't see coming at this point uh the investigation you know felt like it was mostly over all
the major problems were fixed but mobile was still sitting just outside our target and I was you know really scraping the bottom of the barrel for ideas. So I
started reading articles about some common performance patterns and one that kept coming up was preloading on hover for desktop. So this means that you
start fetching data as soon as a user hovers over a link. So by the time they click the data is already there. Now of
course uh there is no hover on mobile. But you know remember the tap that I mentioned earlier like to open our panel. So when you tap the panel slides
up with an animation before our component is actually ready. So there would be a gap between the tap and the component showing up and that gap I
realized is maybe our version of the hover like a window where we could start fetching early. So you know how big is that gap caused
by the animation like my god said tiny but I had learned my lesson by now so I measured it. I open dev tools, turned on CPU
throttling, you know, to simulate a lower-end phone. And when I turned that on, I was surprised like it took up to a full second like, you know, a full
second just sitting there doing nothing useful. The app is busy resizing the canvas, you know, sliding up the tray, mounting our component, but the network
is completely free. So you know the the idea was simple which is to fire off our request during that dead time. So you know it's just one network call without
heavy JavaScript. We wouldn't make anything slower. We just use you know the time that was being wasted. So I built it and we shipped it and the
improvement was huge. Like we saved over 500 milliseconds and just like that iOS performance was fully green. That left us with a final engineering
challenge. So, Android, our P90 was green, but P50 wasn't quite there yet. So, we decided to try one last ambitious idea like what if we prefetched the
recommendation the moment a user selects uh any text element instead of waiting for the tap. We built it, but the results were weird. So the time spent on
the network calls went down significantly just as we expected. Uh but the overall time remained completely flat. So all that time that we had saved
on the network mysteriously reappeared on the client side again. We couldn't explain it this time. So we dropped the investigation and moved on to some other
things. But the story has a nice ending. Like a few weeks later, uh the host app team like the Adobe Express team shipped an our related update and suddenly our
Android performance jumped on its own. We checked a few hypothesis uh for why, but none of them held up. We never figured out, you know, exactly what
changed on their end, but honestly, we didn't have time to investigate why something got better, so we just took the win. So you know that that last bottleneck
had been outside our code all along. So you know from three times over target to green pretty much everywhere. So now there is one more thing that I
want to share which is how I navigated all of this behind the scenes. So throughout this investigation I needed help from people on other teams like
people I had never worked with before often with little time zone overlap. A lot of the time, you know, I wasn't jumping on a call. I was writing a
message that had to make sense on its own. So, that got me thinking about how I write those messages. And I kept coming back to the same idea
like take the work of the other person. Don't make them dig for what you need. I started sending like weekly updates to about 10 15 people, you know, a short
headline and a pie chart, you know, up front for anyone just keeping tabs and there would be a full technical breakdown uh in the thread reply for the
people, you know, actually working on the problem with me. So, you know, same pie chart updated every week. So, anyone could just glance at it and see the
progress. And if I thought that someone might mind uh misunderstand what a number actually means, I would add the note before they even had to ask.
And you know, this paid off in ways that I did not expect. Like for example, my director specifically called out those pie charts like he said he could follow
the entire investigation just from them. And also at one point the program manager uh for our entire organization reached out to give positive feedback.
I had never spoken to her on a call, so she'd been just following along silently uh the whole time. So, you know, people notice, like even the people you don't
realize are watching. And when you need help from another team, it's a lot easier to get it if they already have the context. So, that didn't make things
faster because the investigation still took about 4 months, but it made it possible. Now uh this whole story took place about a year ago and of course the tooling has
changed a lot since then like for example the models are a lot better at explaining things now like a year ago I wouldn't have
trusted an AI to explain I don't know course prefet mechanics CDN cache fragmentation today I probably would so you know the learning part is
genuinely faster but you know here's Here's the thing like remember that cache trap you know the fact that desktop and mobile share the CDN in our specific setup no model
is going to know that on its own unless you know to uh how to tell it. So you know uh some of these performance
problems are really really niche and you still need to convince another team to prioritize your request so that's not a prompt engineering problem. So you know of course use the tools like
they are good and getting better fast but that judgment knowing what to ask like knowing what context actually matters that's still on you uh and that judgment like knowing where
to look knowing who to ask is really what this whole journey came down to. So you know if I had to distill it into
three ideas it would be these. So first off, trust data, not intuition. Uh it will often surprise you and lead you to the real problem.
Secondly, think in systems. The biggest problems are often hiding at the boundaries between our teams. And finally, communicate constantly because it's the best way to solve
problems that involve multiple teams. So that's my story. Thank you for listening. >> [applause] >> U if you'd like to connect like that's my LinkedIn on the screen. Uh and I
would be happy to answer any questions. >> First of all, thank you for the talk. Yes, there is one short question. How do you gather performance analytics?
>> Uh yeah, that's a good question. So the process is as follows. The product manager uh decides what's important performance-wise for the feature. In our
case, it was how long it takes to show a font to display it. It's fully loaded. And then we have to write the code that
actually measures that. You know the metrics are collected for for all the users that uh use our component and they get to uh you know analytics collection
tool and then we can make queries on it and analyze the data as we need. >> Thank you. There are no further questions. Let's thank the speaker Luca
again. Thank you. >> Yeah. Thank you. [applause]
